Treatment A has a higher success rate than Treatment B among mild cases, AND a higher success rate than Treatment B among severe cases. Yet when both groups are combined, Treatment B has the higher overall success rate. How is this possible?
choices: It isn't possible — one of the two group results must be a calculation error
Treatment A is used disproportionately on severe cases (which have lower success rates for both treatments), skewing its combined average downward
The paradox only works if the treatments are actually identical
Success rates cannot be averaged across groups of different sizes

questions.q: A pilot who flies poorly is scolded harshly and flies better next time. A pilot who flies excellently is praised and flies more averagely next time. An instructor concludes scolding works better than praise. What is the more likely statistical explanation?
choices: Scolding is genuinely more effective at improving performance
Praise causes overconfidence that harms performance
Pilots deliberately underperform after praise to appear humble
Regression to the mean: unusually poor or excellent performances tend to be followed by more typical ones, regardless of any feedback given

questions.q: A coin is rolled without slipping around the outside of another identical, stationary coin until it returns to its starting point. Naively, since the two coins have equal circumference, you might guess it spins exactly once. How many times does it actually rotate about its own center?
In a room of just 23 randomly chosen people, is the probability that at least two of them share a birthday closer to 6%, 50%, or 90%? (Ignore leap years; assume birthdays are uniformly distributed.)

During WWII, researchers studying returning fighter planes found bullet holes concentrated on the wings and tail, with almost none on the engine or cockpit. The initial instinct was to armor the areas with the most holes. Statistician Abraham Wald argued for armoring the areas with NO holes instead. Why?
choices: Enemy gunners were specifically trained to avoid the engine and cockpit
The undamaged planes in the sample had simply flown fewer missions
Planes hit in the engine or cockpit were shot down and never returned to be examined, so the missing holes marked the truly fatal locations
The engine and cockpit were already bulletproof by design
